speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Clerk will now proceed to read the Order of the Day.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But sanctity of contract is also not absolute, and intervention is needed when there is a need to safeguard the fundamental integrity of our economic structure for the common good.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It recognised the reality of the situation: that almost nobody, no one, could have anticipated or prepared for the impact of COVID-19 in Singapore and in the world.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The assumptions that one had made in entering into those contracts at the time they did, went out the window with COVID-19.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If we did not intervene and people insisted on strict contractual rights in respect of contracts made prior to the onset of COVID-19, many would suffer.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Good businesses could go under; bankruptcies and insolvencies could rise dramatically.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, we moved this Bill, first in April, and subsequently, in June, we made further refinements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The fundamental idea underpinning the reliefs was that a fair sharing of obligations would be necessary given the exceptional times that we found ourselves in.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Without such an arrangement, many SMEs would suffer and it would be detrimental to our economy as a whole.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Bill today builds on the reliefs that we have already put in place by ensuring that they can be implemented more smoothly and more efficiently and to make sure that the reliefs get to the ground in the best possible way.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The first is to make a number of technical amendments to facilitate the implementation and the delivery of reliefs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, it introduces temporary measures for the Minister to extend certain collective sale deadlines on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In April, we introduced temporary and targeted measures to alleviate the impact on parties who are unable to perform their contractual obligations because of COVID-19.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This was the legal circuit breaker that we had implemented, to temporarily hold in abeyance the imposition of strict legal rights and strict enforcement of legal rights.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It was intended to give businesses at that point in time some cash flow relief, some breathing space to find the possibility of negotiating a mutual and acceptable settlement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We set up the Panel of Assessors for COVID-19 Temporary Relief, or PACT, to adjudicate disputes quickly and effectively between the parties, taking into account the particular circumstances that exist between the parties and having, ultimately, regard to the justice of the situation between the parties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: PACT Assessors were, therefore, empowered to make determinations which were just and equitable in the circumstances.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We also introduced measures to facilitate alternative meeting arrangements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This ensured that organisations and entities could continue to fulfil their regulatory as well as corporate governance functions, even when personal attendance at meetings might not be viable or safe due to the safe distancing measures that we had put in place.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In June 2020, we introduced a rental relief framework for SMEs and specified non-profit organisations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This addressed the growing need to provide tenants with immediate rental relief from their accumulated rental obligations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The rental relief framework mandated an equitable co-sharing of rental obligations between the Government, landlords and tenants.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It provided additional rental relief for tenants who are substantially impacted by COVID-19, and also facilitated the appointment of a panel of rental relief Assessors to consider the disputes between the parties in the manner I outlined earlier.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The relief measures have been a lifeline for many Singaporeans and local businesses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, out of the slightly more than 7,000, about 1,200 had sought assessments by Assessors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Out of this number, almost 60% of them has been disposed of in the space of about four months.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The reason we believe why there is a much smaller number of applications for assessments than there are Notifications for Relief is because we provided a framework in the legislation for parties to assess for themselves what might work for them and we encouraged them actively to look within that framework to find a solution without having to come to Assessors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Most of the determinations have been issued quickly and from the day an application for an Assessor’s determination is filed, parties can generally expect the determination to be issued within four weeks, if they file the documents requested and also provide the substantiation for the claims that they make.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Some cases take a little longer because the nature of the case is a bit more complicated and more complex.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, the measures that we have put in place in April and in June ought to be looked at and seen in the context of the other measures that are also put in place to assist businesses and to assist employees as well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Feedback from the businesses on the measures so far have been positive, and for what it is worth, there have been some surveys done by UOB, Accenture, and Dun and Bradstreet – these are not commissioned by the Government or MinLaw.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On the rental relief front, we have been actively engaging landlords and SME tenants, both before the Bill was constructed, as well as after that, to continue the engagement process to explain how it works and to assist with ironing out problems on the ground.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This Bill today does not introduce major changes to the policy framework and to the intent that I have outlined, but makes a number of clarificatory and also technical amendments to facilitate a better delivery of the reliefs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We gleaned many of these from interacting with the Assessors, understanding how we can better deliver the services on the ground, and also appreciating the process which has taken place in the last few months.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 8 expands the powers of the rental relief Assessors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At present, only three distinct matters may be determined by a rental relief Assessor.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, whether the tenant satisfies the prescribed criteria to qualify for rental relief.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, whether the tenant satisfies the prescribed additional criteria for the additional relief.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, there are two layers – basic and the additional.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Thirdly, whether the landlord satisfies the criteria for the reduction of the additional rental relief – that is the landlord relief portion.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will address instances where service or maintenance charges are not broken down under the lease agreement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The reason for this, if I may explain to Members, is that the relief that has been given – two months from the Government and two months from the landlords – cover the base rent without the charges.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The reason for not requiring the landlords to waive the charges is because these charges continue to be due to the service providers in the form of maintenance or utilities charges.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Sometimes, the lease agreement itself might not stipulate which portion is the base rent and which portion are the service charges.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These amendments seek to empower the Assessors to make a determination as to which portion ought to be waived.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In addition, the Rental Relief Regulations, which I am sure Members have studied carefully, also provide a series of formula which applies to the different scenarios for rental relief waivers to take place; sometimes, depending on when the tenant has moved in or moved out, or whether or not the business is of one nature or another, depending on the criteria.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is to enlarge the power so that should an Assessor come across these cases, it will not lack the jurisdiction to address all of these disputes holistically.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: When it comes into force, Part 8 will provide relief for prescribed contracts that have been affected by delays in construction, supply or related contracts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This was introduced in light of the severe impact that COVID-19 had on the construction industry.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The extent to which a tenant is able or unable in some cases to move in because of the landlord's inability to renovate or retrofit; these are scenarios that could be captured in Part 8.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Part 8 will, in turn, allow assessors limited prescribed powers to adjust the terms of a contract that has been impacted by COVID-19.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, in the scenario I outlined, should there be a reason for not being able to allow the tenant to move in in time, because you have not made good the premises, the assessors can make some adjustments to the contract.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The overriding and overarching consideration is to achieve a just and equitable outcome for both parties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To give one further example, a contractor may have rented equipment from a supplier and the equipment is un-used during the circuit breaker because the site was closed as would have been the case for much of the circuit breaker period.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There can be significant unfairness in this situation if the contractor must continue to pay rental even though he was unable to use the equipment throughout the period because of COVID-19 restrictions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Some suppliers that we spoke to, said that they would waive the rental for the period where the contractor cannot use the equipment due to COVID-19 restrictions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They felt that it was not right for them to continue charging rental at the expense of the contractor.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For many of these, we applaud these suppliers for responding to COVID-19 in the right spirit and certainly in the context of assisting holistically, the entire industry.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the same time, we have also come across many situations where suppliers continue to insists on the full rental throughout the period despite the conditions prevailing at that point in time.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is where Part 8 can come in, to play a part to resolve the matter in a just and equitable manner between the parties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I would emphasise to Members that the powers of the Assessor in this context are narrowly defined.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The categories of contracts that the Assessor can adjust under Part 8 are circumscribed by subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Further, the applicants will also be required to show that the contract was affected in the first place by a delay in the performance of a construction or supply contract and was otherwise in breach, and this was materially caused by COVID-19 related restrictions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Parties would also have an opportunity to be heard before the Assessor on any points of disagreement between the claimant and the respondent, before the Assessor makes a decision.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The assessment process will also be subject to a rigorous review internally.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And if I may share with Members, in the last few months, we have had many briefings with the Assessors so that there is alignment across the process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Both Minister Shanmugam and myself have also met with Assessors to go through the cases and we do that on a regular basis to achieve alignment and a fair degree of consistency across the cases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In this Bill, we have provided for how proceedings and the determination under Part 8 will interact with other legal proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is necessary as otherwise, there could be parallel proceedings, one under Part 8 of this Bill and another under either SOPA or as a case may be, in judicial proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The moratorium will therefore apply until the Part 8 application is rejected or withdrawn, or until a determination has been issued.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will, as I mentioned earlier, mitigate and reduce the risk of parallel proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In the construction industry, many contracting parties rely on SOPA adjudication proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This applies as long as the contract has not been previously gone through the Part 8 process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In other words, you cannot go through Part 8, get a result, perhaps not happy with it and then apply for a further adjustment go through the SOPA proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This amendment, in empowering the SOPA adjudicators the same bandwidth as the Assessors to make the same adjustments, will allow for SOPA adjudicators to also have the same ability to reach a just and equitable outcome in those cases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In many of these SOPA cases, the issues are similar, across whether or not the performance has been affected by an event like COVID-19 and whether or not the payments are due and how much is due and at what stage.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Because of the twinning of these issues that arise in such typical SOPA claims, we felt that it was appropriate to clothe the SOPA adjudicator with the same level of discretion and also powers to make those adjudications.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Government is committed to working closely with the industry to get through this difficult period.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I must say that we will do all we can to continue to cushion the impact of COVID-19 on the industry and to help the industry emerge from this as best as we can and perhaps stronger from the crisis.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Part 4 provides for alternative arrangements to enable meetings to be held by electronic means, where personal attendance would otherwise have been required.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Members would know that many entities, whether large corporates or smaller societies or charities they do not have a constitutional document that would automatically allow them to hold virtual meetings without physical presence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These arrangements are therefore critical for those entities to allow them to carry on business and also to proceed with governance functions and obligations safely through this pandemic.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They can proceed with their meetings virtually and also, through that virtual platform, make important collective decisions while still complying with safe distancing regulations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The alternative arrangements are currently linked to the duration of a control order.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have received feedback that this creates some uncertainty because some companies have their Financial Year end at the end of this year and they have until March or April to hold their meetings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Many of these entities must plan for these meetings months in advance and make the appropriate arrangements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It enables alternative arrangements to be prescribed if the Minister for Law considers it necessary or expedient to limit or prevent the spread of COVID-19, even where there is no control order in force, for the purposes of these alternative arrangements for meetings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This would cover the period of time that I mentioned earlier for all the meetings to take place, including in the context of some, the adjourned meetings as well, up till June 2021.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The possibility of a further extension might be considered but we can take that assessment depending on the prevailing conditions subsequently.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This extension will give entities the option to hold virtual meetings in place of physical meetings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Lastly, Sir, the Bill also introduces further amendments to the Registrar's powers, in response to feedback from the PACT Registry in operationalising the Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These amendments seek to facilitate the efficient and effective operation of the Act and will apply to both the PACT Registry and the Rental Relief Registry.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The PACT Registry deals with the COVID-19 Bill as we passed in April and the Rental Relief Registry deals with the ones we passed in June this year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Currently, the Registrars have the power to reject applications that do not comply with the form and manner prescribed by the regulations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: What the Registrars and Assessors have seen has been certain defective applications which have come through, not falling within the original prescription, but nonetheless, defective or failed in some way.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These applications still make their way through the system because there is no power to dismiss them ab initio, as of right.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They, therefore, drain the time and resources of the Registry and also the volunteer Assessors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Members would know that this closely aligns with the kinds of standards that we prescribe for filing papers in judicial proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Bill also makes certain clarificatory amendments, in line with the Regulations which have been promulgated.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Section 7A provides for a cap on late payment interest and charges.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There was some doubt as to whether the time period when this cap would apply, so we made that clear.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Chia proposed extending the statutory repayment schemes beyond rental arrears, to help businesses who want to restart.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Currently, we have a statutory repayment scheme that applies only to rental arrears but Mr Chia is proposing that we go beyond this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are aware of this suggestion, it has been raised with us.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But, we wanted to proceed very carefully because this opens up a significant amount of outstandings that will be subject to the repayment schedule or that could be termed out in the repayment schedule, possibly to the detriment of creditors as well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, we want to balance the cash flow needs of these creditors against those businesses who have fallen into debt.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will study this further and determine if this is appropriate and if so, on what kind of scale.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Chia also made reference to whether we could provide relief for Directors from liability for insolvent trading in this period.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Chia would be pleased to know that the Bill already covers that, in fact, the Act has been passes in April.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It already covers that and a company is not treated as incurring liabilities without a reasonable prospect of meeting them in full during the prescribed period, and that is the threshold for insolvent trading liability for an individual director.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will also cover deadlines that have already passed, provided that the other requirements for extension are met.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This measure is intended to address feedback from some Collective Sale Committees or "CSCs", that they require extensions to the deadlines specified in the Land Titles Strata Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ordinarily, these deadlines ensure that the CSC follows through with the collective sale process in a timely manner, minimising uncertainty for the owners in the development.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: However, we have received feedback from CSCs that their ability to complete the collective sale process could have been genuinely and also materially impacted by COVID-19.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, they may have been unable to secure a buyer due to travel restrictions for instance and also possibly the circuit breaker measures.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: All applications for extension will be evaluated carefully, and only those cases where the CSC has been genuinely and materially impacted by COVID-19 will an extension be granted.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The process and procedure for such an application will be set out in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Over the past few months, as Members would appreciate, we had to respond very quickly to the pandemic.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have had to be agile, act quickly, provide effective relief to businesses and individuals, to help as far as possible, to cushion the impact of COVID-19.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So far we have seen encouraging and tangible results from the reliefs that were introduced in the first two rounds.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have seen how the Act has provided breathing spaces and also provide for there to be a way in which the two parties, as I mentioned earlier, can use a framework that is published in the Legislation to work through their own difficulties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The numbers, I think, bear out that proposition.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker, I beg to move.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The rental relief measures introduced as an amendment to COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) Act in June 2020 represents one of the hallmarks of the Government's decisive response in mitigating the effects of COVID-19 pandemic on individuals and small businesses.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The targeted relief has an impact of producing cost and improving cash flow, which we all know, is the lifeline of companies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As I understand these are tenants who have suffered at least a 35% drop in revenue over the April-May 2020 period this year compared to the corresponding period last year.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Assessors appointed under this Act, in my respectful view, form the backbone of the implementation of this Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We are fortunate that a good number of professionals drawn from law, accountancy and tax practices have stepped forward to help in this huge endeavour in the midst of the crisis that no doubt would have affected them too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They are paid a token honorarium but have and will continue to put in quite a lot of time and effort in the discharge of their important duties.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Being drawn from the professions, they bring with them credibility too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To each of them, we owe a debt of gratitude in answering the call for our nation, and I join the hon Minister in thanking them too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, I note with interest that the hon Minister himself has been involved in briefing sessions with them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now move on to the impact of the Act on smaller landlords.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister Shanmugam recognised the potential plight of the smaller landlords who rely on rent for their livelihoods in his June 2020.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For such landlords, they can apply for an assessment to provide half of the additional relief required.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have anecdotally received feedback on potential hardship that may be visited on these landlords arising from two general situations.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The first is a timing mismatch between when IRAS provides the property tax rebate and the tenant's decision in not paying the rent equivalent to the rebate as provided for under the Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, the decisions on the part of tenants not to pay rent amounting to the full extent of the additional rental relief available under the Act not taking into account the landlord's status as a small landlord.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wonder if the hon Minister could please shed light on how these affected landlords may be assisted on the possibly unintended consequences of this Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, I note that the hon Minister, Minister Shanmugam acknowledged in the MinLaw's Addendum to the President's speech that in the coming months, some companies will face a real risk of insolvency and financial constraints may cause litigants to forgo pursuing their legal rights.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He also intends to introduce in this House cost-effective measures for small businesses to restructure or wind-up.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: All of us in this House must recognise that these are tough times.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There are no easy solutions in this area of providing rental relief to individuals and organisations impacted by the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There will be more muscular organisations which will not be happy with the relief measures under this Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, the pitching of the legislative policy must always be in favour of greater good of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This amendment Bill continues to strike that appropriate balance.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Deputy Speaker, in the past few months the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) Act imposed on landlords the obligation to pass on property tax rebates and waive rentals to benefit tenants who are SMEs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These measures rewrote the tenancy agreements they had entered causing income disruption to landlords.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These interventions were meant to support business tenants and help them pull through the circuit breaker which disrupted their businesses.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In August, IRAS had sent her a notification of cash grant and rental waivers informing her of the grant she was to receive and the fact that she was to provide four months of rental waivers to her tenant.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This lady was in her 90s and in an extremely poor health, who moved out of a landed house to receive rental income to repay a family debt and to fund her daily expenses and medical costs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As the family found that the rental waivers required were too much for them to bear, they came to see me at my Meet-the-People Session for assistance.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I advised them that she should apply for an assessment on account of financial hardship.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If successful, she would only need to provide half of what was initially required that is two months rental waiver.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Section 19M requires the landlord to apply to the Registrar of Assessors within the prescribed time and in the prescribed form in manner.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This assessment would determine, among other things, whether a landlord was entitled to a reduction of the additional rental relief.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Coming back to the example I gave, the resident had to wait a few days to see me, and in fact had only been recently discharged from a hospital.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Her family was also more conversant in Chinese and found going through the requirements novel and onerous.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The application needed to be filed via SingPass to the Singapore Land Authority as the managing agency.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such steps are not so straightforward for some small landlords and probably some tenants as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As such, it is important that the process be user-friendly and that information be easily available in the four major languages.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I will be commenting on these two areas on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The first section I would like to address is clauses 15 to 17 of the Bill, which modifies some of the procedures relating to the Security of Payment Act or SOPA.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The construction industry has been one of those hard hit by the COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Generally, construction contracts are very prescriptive with parties having specific obligations to perform certain works within specific time frames.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Two things are generally of critical importance: time and money.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One of the biggest problems contractors faced, is that if there are delays or issues in a construction project, payment may be withheld by the paying party.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This can be between developer and main contractor or between contractors and their own sub-contractors.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Dispute resolution through courts or arbitration may take time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It was a deal with this process that the Security of Payments Act system was set up, which generally provided a fast way for claimants to recover payments due before full resolution of all disputes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These process requires both the claimants and respondents to adhere to strict timelines to file claims and responses and the adjudication would give a quick decision.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This process has significantly reduced the time and costs of resolving construction disputes and many disputes would not proceed to full hearing after that.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The COVID-19 situation has hit this industry hard and works in many places had to be stopped.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While the current legislation gives contractors moratorium for liabilities arising from delays caused by COVID-19, I expect that now works are gradually resuming, parties will want to be clear that they will be able to recover payment for works, as well as benefit from any necessary COVID-19 reliefs granted by the Act.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think this also harmonises the two Acts by giving adjudicators the same powers as Assessors which makes eminent sense, so two processes are not needed, but this also gives a lot of flexibility to Assessors and adjudicators in modifying the contract, which is not very common in the construction industry, and this may create a lot of legal uncertainties, because there are many, many ways in which contracts may be affected by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The balance that Assessors and adjudicators would need to take is want to make sure that parties are able to perform or enforce bargains they believed they made, but not be penalised by the effect of the moratorium.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The additional time and costs needed for performance of these contracts would also need to be carefully considered because it is not always easy to determine where these should fall, and this is almost always what construction contracts try to do too – place responsibility for losses or delays on one person or the other.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For example, if a project has been delayed for six months and has to be restarted, there will be costs to remobilised, there will be shortages of manpower, higher costs for hiring.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think in many ways, Assessors will have to exercise a lot of discretion on how they are going to allocate these additional costs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If there are any guidelines for Assessors or adjudicators where they should bear in mind, this may be helpful especially in a very prescriptive industry like construction.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The second area I would like to address is clause 12, which relates to Alternative Arrangements for Meetings.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Generally, I have had very good feedback on the provision for these alternative arrangements.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It basically allows AGMs and Board meetings to be held virtually.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The feedback, of course I had, was that the hard deadline that was initially in place made it difficult for companies to plan for AGMs that may take place longer, especially where they need sometime in advance to call AGMs; and sometimes AGMs get adjourned.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The legislation itself gives the Minister discretion to decide how long or short a time frame this legislation is going to be in place for; this amended proceedings.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And I think at the very least three months advance notice would be helpful, a longer period would be even better.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In this regard, there is actually no harm in erring in the side of caution and giving a longer period because I think there is not much downside – even if the COVID situation is better – there is no harm if the virtual meeting provisions are still in place and meetings can go on virtually.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It has, indeed, been a lifeline for many SMEs in these difficult economic times.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I just have a few quick clarifications to seek.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They are not aware of the laws that have been passed and the rental relief they can get.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, some coffeeshop stallholders in Nee Soon East are aware of the rental relief but did not know that it was for four months.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They also do not know where to seek recourse.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Not requiring eligible tenants and sub-tenants again to take any further steps to obtain rental relief is a well-intentioned measure.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, it may be a double-edged sword if it is not accompanied by proactive communication and enforcement of the relief measures to tenants and sub-tenants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to take a more proactive approach to ensure that the rental relief is reaching those who need this lifeline the most.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, what percentage of these complaints are resolved with the rental relief being subsequently provided to the tenants and sub-tenants respectively?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, as some tenants and sub-tenants, especially again the coffeeshop stallholders, still appear to be unaware of their rental relief rights under this framework, can the Minister share if a more comprehensive communication mechanism could be put in place urgently to inform eligible tenants and sub-tenants of such reliefs?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If not, can landlords and tenants be made responsible to show evidence that they have informed their tenants or sub-tenants respectively of their rental reliefs?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Fourth, given the additional rights of the assessor to vary the relief amounts pursuant to this new Bill, can the Minister share what safeguards will be put in place to ensure that tenants and sub-tenants have sufficient clarity from the outset of the rental relief and amounts that they should be entitled to?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Similar to my earlier point, how will MinLaw be communicating this to the tenants and sub-tenants?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I declare my interest as a corporate dispute lawyer and sitting on boards of several charities and companies.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Members of my firm are also volunteers of the assessor team.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The amendments, as proposed in the Bill, are timely and, in particular, the amendments to section 27 of the Act in relation to the alternative meeting arrangements for organisations during the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With the extension to June 2021, this is greatly welcomed as it avoids several difficulties.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The present amendment, which will pave the way forward for an extension of timeline, is also welcomed by organisations and charities as well.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, I am proposing whether the Government can look into how we can incorporate such alternative meeting arrangements on a long-term basis, embedded as part of our companies' and charities' legislative and regulatory framework beyond this COVID-19 period, beyond a temporary basis.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The feedback I have received and my own experience are that these alternative meeting arrangements have proven to be not only cost-efficient but effective as it compels meetings to prioritise and focus on the business at hand.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Indeed, COVID-19 has precipitated and necessitated the digital adoption and transformation of our organisations.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But having taken the first steps of the digitalisation journey, we should adopt a framework that would encourage organisations to continue to forge ahead with the digitalisation journey for our organisations.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Malay):   	In my experience as a former Director of the Singapore Malay Chamber of Commerce and Industry (DPPMS), an alternative platform for holding meetings was a most welcomed one.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is because most of the DPPMS members are businessmen or micro-SMEs and, by allowing AGMs to be held through alternative platforms, such as online communications, this can help lower their costs because many of our enterprises have spread their wings to either regional or international markets.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, when I was a Director at AMP, we have studied how digital transformation can be implemented in our Malay/Muslim welfare organisations.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Through COVID-19 and the amendments to the Act, many more organisations can make use of this opportunity to undergo digital transformation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English) Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, in conclusion, I support the amendments.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will be the start of our digitalisation movement towards alternative meeting arrangements as our organisations become more global in nature and members are situated anywhere around the world.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Further, this will stand us in good stead to be prepared for future crises.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The changes to the Bill will help to provide clarity to Singapore's legal intervention.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Over the last few weeks, several tenants and landlords have approached me with regard to rental disputes.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Many have longstanding relationships with one another but could not find an amicable way to resolve.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This has been further amplified by the economic challenges faced across various industries.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I commend the efforts of the MinLaw team, along with other Ministries and agencies, who continue to review the Act to ensure that it remains relevant to this ever-changing COVID-19 situation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked how many assessors have been appointed and what steps have been taken to ensure that they perform their duties well and how are they trained for that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I have explained earlier, we do have regular discussions with them – myself, Minister Shanmugam and also the MinLaw officers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In that way, we keep a parity and we ensure that the decisions are also consistent with each other across the different panels.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There are 12 panels and each of them is headed by a senior District Judge from the State Courts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The MinLaw team also conducts daily check-in sessions with the PACT Registry to provide guidance on the cases filed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, not only on the cases that have been looked at or assessed, but the cases filed, to get a sense as to whether or not there needs to be improvement to the way in which we administer and operationalise the way in which the registry functions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai also asked whether there have been plans to extend the moratorium order under the current Act, which is due to expire on 19 October 2020 and how such a possible extension might be balanced against the interests of both parties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In answering the second question, first, we have to bear in mind that, as I have said, it is intrusive to step in to intervene into parties' contracts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we do that judiciously and we always have to keep an eye on whether or not it is appropriate, what is the right level of intervention and whether, in the first place, the circumstances require that intervention.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we will monitor that carefully to make an assessment based on prevailing circumstances, whether that is still necessary.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But I just want to cite, for the Member's information, that we have seen a general downward trend in the number of Notifications For Reliefs that have been filed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: From July to August, compared to May and June, we have seen a downward trend.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This suggests to us that either the number of cases has been coming down in terms of the disputes or, as I have postulated at the start, the cases have come down partly also because there is not even a need to file an NFR, given that the framework has become a little bit better socialised to the public and people know what the framework provides for and, therefore, can negotiate on their own accord outside of the NFR regime altogether.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we will monitor that, together with the prevailing circumstances, to assess whether or not we need to extend the moratorium.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai also asked about the total value of the rental rebate that the commercial, industrial and office tenants have received and what is the estimated additional rental rebate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Government's assistance for the rental relief component comprises both the property tax rebate for 2020 and also the cash grant from the Government.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, in total, these are the two components which make up the grants given in respect of the rental relief framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is worth noting that both components of the Government support are calculated based on the annual value of the property and that might not exactly be the same amount of the rental waivers that individual landlords provide.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I have mentioned earlier, the annual value is the approximated annual return that the property is expected to fetch.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But what the market or what the landlord might get out of that particular property might well be different.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And the other, of course, is the waivers are only in respect of the base rent or contractual rent and not the service and utility charges.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng raised several concerns in his usual quickfire fashion and I will try and replicate a quickfire response.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, on the construct of the scheme and whether tenants are aware or not aware, and whether it is easy to use.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We did receive some feedback that in having to pass down the property tax rebate from the Government to landlord, landlord to tenants, there might be some friction in that process, which is why this scheme that we have designed that was passed in June does not rely on that "passing the parcel" as it were, but simply by way of notification from IRAS.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Once that notification kicks in, then it applies by way of waivers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it is not so much what you have to pass down but rather what the tenants do not have to pay for the relevant period.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it is deliberately designed in this way to ensure that, as far as possible, no active step needs to be taken by the tenant.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, Mr Louis Ng asked what if landlords are either slow or failed to inform their tenants.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have a framework that is set in place.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have prescribed that but, obviously, there are also roughness at the edges – some might not know that they have received it, some might be unable to find their tenant for a period of time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They may not be operating their business and so on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we understand that and all that is taken into account.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But there is a default framework that applies absent anything else.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think it is a highly relevant point.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The whole idea is for people to understand what the framework provides for and to be able to use the framework in a way which applies to them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have put up the usual infographics, we have explained it as best as we can, we have also taken to having a dedicated website just to explain this and put all the materials at one place.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Both Minister Shanmugam and myself have conducted several webinars and sessions, in some cases, face-to-face, some cases on online portals to explain this to people who then pass on the information.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, we have sat down with several merchants associations and federations so that they in turn can pass down the information to their members and in that way disseminate it.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we try as best as we can to plug into these networks and try and explain and give information.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have also used community means, through organisations on the ground, using business associations, giving them the materials.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And, ultimately, if they do have questions after all of this, we do have a team; it has been highly stretched but we do have a team that sits and takes calls and explains and also walks through the process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Later on, when I address Ms Lim's points about timing and about not being too strict, I will also explain further what else our officers do to assist in this programme.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked about some landlords who may have financial difficulty and may face difficulties themselves.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, one month for industrial/office and two months for commercial.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: You compare that and if you have a 35% drop, the additional relief kicks in.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is only the additional relief that the landlords are obliged to bear.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We fix it at 60,000 because that is the median annual value of commercial properties in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Based on these numbers, we expect that it does cover a fair number and if one is holding to the properties that exceeds the median annual value of commercial properties in Singapore, then you might not qualify or you would not qualify for the scheme.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would not say it captures everyone, but by and large in hardship cases, you are likely to fall within this framework, you will get the relief from the Assessors and the landlords, those who think that they can qualify, should apply for assessment by the Assessors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On top of that, as we have explained, and as Mr Shanmugam explained when this Bill was introduced in June, there are also other softer measures, such as the bank loans and forbearance and other measures that working through MAS, the banks have offered.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked about process timing and whether parties who filed appeals or filed applications out of time, whether or not that would be taken against them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We look at the substance of the case and the merits of the case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Registrar has a discretion to accept applications out of time and will do so as long as there is merit in the application, there is good reason and it is not a frivolous reason.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition our officers also often receive requests for clarification, either on the phone or in person or online.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On occasion our officers also proactively assist the applicants in form filling or in explaining the process and procedure so that they will be able to have their applications either for rental relief or for landlords' additional relief to be heard by the Assessors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, I wish to assure Ms Sylvia Lim that this is being done already and if she is aware of any other cases which fall through the cracks, which require assistance, please do reach out to us and we will assist.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Vikram Nair asked some questions about SOPA – about the timing and the cash flow.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We understand that SOPA is really designed to ensure that there is security of payment and cash flow is critical in the industry.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The provisions in this Bill do not affect the timeline in SOPA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: All we are saying is as long as you have got an application for determination filed under Part 8 of this Act, then do not duplicate the process by also asking for relief in SOPA and I think that is a fair position to take.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: You do not get two bites at the cherry for relief.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As far as guidelines are concerned for Assessors and adjudicators, the same briefings, the same guidance we give to the current Assessors, we will also give to the SOPA adjudicators.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Those who are given the same ambit of powers of discussion as the current PACT Assessors, they will also be given the same guidance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Vikram Nair spoke about it, Mr Zhulkarnain also spoke about it and I think the proof of the pudding is in the eating.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think if you are asking for this on a permanent basis, it cannot be quite a bad thing.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I just want to point out that actually under the Companies Act, as long as the constitutional documents or the memorandum and articles of the company or the relevant organisation, provides for it, then you can, in fact, already hold your meetings in a non-physical manner.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There needs to be some compliance with the Companies Act and different companies or different societies may have slightly different obligations to fulfil.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But by and large the scheme is there, the regime is there.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If you are able to take advantage of it because your own constitution allows for it, then you can do so.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They can continue to make those arrangements and beyond that we will make an assessment.
